articles.title: US Homeland Security Intimidates Border Tribe with Surveillance
articles.content: Promising Cooperation: The Tohono O’odham Nation sued to stop a wall from being built on their land. In court, DHS gave assurances that the government would engage with the tribe in good faith. Intimidation Tactics: ProPublica found that DHS has surveilled an ongoing border prayer ceremony and questioned tribal members outside the reservation.  Border Security: Despite steep declines in border crossings, officials describe the tribe’s land in Southern Arizona as “one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors.” These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story. At 4:59 a.m. on Aug. 25, Verlon Jose, the chairman of the Tohono O’odham Nation in Southern Arizona, received an email from the head of the U.S. Border Patrol’s Tucson Sector. Government contractors were en route to conduct soil tests for construction of a 62-mile wall along the Nation’s southern boundary, wrote acting chief patrol agent Henry N. Laxdal. If the tribe wished to have cultural monitors observe the work, they were welcome to, but they could not interfere with the government’s operations. The work would begin in exactly one minute. Jose, 59, was already aware of the contractors’ arrival. An hour earlier, a tribal member had called to report a caravan heading south through the reservation, and Facebook was lighting up with similar accounts. The convoy included not only work trucks and drilling rigs, but Border Patrol vehicles as well. Dozens of border wall contractor and Border Patrol vehicles pass the Tadai Me:i prayer camp on the morning of Aug. 27. Nate Sosa For months, the O’odham had maneuvered to avoid such a scene, taking their case to federal court. Their homeland straddles the border, and thousands of tribal members live in Mexico. A wall would disrupt routine border crossings for ceremonies and family visits and destroy landscapes they consider their duty to protect, members and leaders say. Their lawsuit argued that the Trump administration’s efforts to build it despite their opposition constituted an historic attack on tribal sovereignty. But administration attorneys gave assurances that the government was engaging with the O’odham in good faith, and a judge in Washington, D.C., denied the tribe’s request for a preliminary injunction. In his Aug. 25 email providing Jose a 60-second heads up, the Border Patrol chief said his agency’s willingness to accommodate cultural monitors underscored its “commitment to ongoing coordination” with the Nation. As daylight broke, Jose learned the contractors were guarded by federal agents in masks and tactical gear, drawn from a special operations cadre that participated in citywide sweeps in Minneapolis and Chicago the previous year, which left three people dead, including two U.S. citizens. When the tribe’s chief of police tried to reach the worksite, he was stopped at a roadblock set up by the agents. Merrian Felix Davy Cross Border Patrol tactical team members amass around the Tadai Me:i prayer camp on Aug. 26. Jose issued a statement on the Nation’s website declaring the incursion illegal and revealing that the Department of Homeland Security had deployed a surveillance blimp and enlisted Mexican security forces to help protect the work crews. For a quarter-century, Tohono O’odham leaders have staved off a border wall by allowing DHS to use the reservation as a testing ground for some of the government’s most aggressive homeland security measures — from vehicle barriers on the reservation’s southern boundary, to state-of-the-art surveillance towers , to law enforcement partnerships with the Border Patrol and Immigration and Customs Enforcement . Despite the collaborations, and assurances from the Trump administration, ProPublica found that DHS has turned its vast apparatus on tribal members, with 24-hour surveillance directed at an ongoing border prayer ceremony and tribal members being questioned outside the reservation about their ceremonial activities. ProPublica’s account is based on photos, videos, court filings, interviews with tribal leadership, firsthand observations and more than 1,000 contemporaneously written observations compiled by tribal members. The battle over a border wall on the Nation has broken along familiar partisan lines in Arizona. While GOP legislative leaders have filed briefs in support of the project, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs has done the same in support of the tribe. Progressive U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, whose district includes the reservation, has said she is crafting legislation to rein in the Department of Homeland Security’s sweeping powers to waive federal laws in order to expedite wall construction. The Trump administration has used those authorities to circumvent environmental and cultural preservation statutes on 60 occasions across its two terms. For Deshane Gregg, whose vehicle was forced off the road by a convoy of contractors and federal agents, the recent show of force on the reservation has felt like a government siege, not cooperation. “You just feel helpless. You see these people, and they’re just so aggressive. They want you to react. They want you to show them that we could be ugly too,” she said. “We’re just here doing prayer. We’re just here, not trying to bother them, but it gets to you when it’s constantly being like that.” “The drones flying over us all day,” she added, “it’s a lot.” A drone hovers over the Tadai Me:i camp during morning prayer songs on Aug. 27. Ryan Devereaux/ProPublica ProPublica sent DHS, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, and the Border Patrol nearly 30 questions about the government’s surveillance and interactions with tribal members and leaders. The agencies answered none of those questions. Instead, CBP pointed to a statement Commissioner Rodney Scott made in August, in which he described the reservation’s southern boundary as “one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border” and a “remote desert that has facilitated decades of drug loads, migrant deaths, and cartel activity.” Regarding construction of a wall, Scott said, “Congress funded this work, a Federal court has affirmed it, and CBP is carrying it out under the legal authorities that apply. Under President Trump’s leadership, we are securing the border and giving our agents the tools and support they need to protect the American people.” A post on X from James Percival, general counsel of the Department of Homeland Security, celebrates the denial of a request for an emergency injunction against border wall construction filed by Tohono O’odham leadership in August. Screenshot of X With no sign the White House or the O’odham government is backing down, DHS has cast off any pretense that the agency will work cooperatively with the Nation. Within hours of the judge’s denial of the emergency injunction, on Aug. 14, the department’s general counsel, James Percival, posted a celebratory meme depicting one of the cybernetic Star Trek supervillains known as “the Borg.” “RESISTANCE IS FUTILE,” it read. “We respect tribal sovereignty but not to the detriment of border security,” he wrote. “This wall is getting built. Our authority is beyond dispute.” The O’odham have inhabited the Sonoran Desert, from what is now Southern Arizona to Mexico’s Sea of Cortez, for thousands of years . According to the tribe, roughly 14,000 of its 37,000 enrolled members live on tribal land west of Tucson. Approximately 3,000 more reside in Mexico. At 2.8 million acres, their reservation is the largest on the southern border by a long shot. During President Donald Trump’s first term, Arizona saw 226 miles of border wall built, but the Nation maintained its status as the longest unwalled section in the state. Confirmation that things would be different this time came in February, when CBP informed the tribe that it planned to seal off the reservation entirely, tapping nearly $52 billion from Trump’s so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act. A vehicle barrier marks the U.S. border with Mexico in the Chukut Kuk District of the Tohono O’odham Nation. Cam Mackey The tribe’s elected leaders met with DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin in hopes of changing the administration’s mind. As an enrolled citizen of the Cherokee Nation, Mullin is the first Native American to head the department. “Maybe we can work with this guy,” Jose recalled thinking. But Mullin’s message was clear: We want to work with you, but we’re building the wall. Justice Department attorneys were prepared to defend the project to the Supreme Court. O’odham council member Vivian Juan-Saunders, who also attended the April 21 meeting, recalls the secretary saying, “Don’t mess with me.” Mullin’s office did not respond to questions from ProPublica, including about the exchange. The message was more direct the following month, when tribal leaders met with Scott. According to Jose, the CBP commissioner told the delegation that if they filed a lawsuit opposing the wall, the Nation could lose access to three border gates members use to travel to and from Mexico. Accessible only to tribal members, the gates are maintained at the discretion of CBP. Juan-Saunders confirmed that CBP threatened to close the gates, as did another council member, Jesse Navarro. CBP declined to comment on the alleged threat. In June, a $1.3 billion contract to build the wall, known as the “Tucson 5” project, was awarded to Sullivan Land Services Co., also known as SLS and SLSCO. The Texas firm has a long history of Republican political donations and was a major recipient of border wall contracts during Trump’s first term. The O’odham filed a lawsuit to stop the project on June 16 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. The tribe contended it would reduce the size of its reservation, which can only be done by Congress — and that the wall would mark an enduring act of trespass on sovereign lands and destroy sacred cultural sites. The administration’s plans cast aside decades of tribal cooperation with DHS, the Nation’s lawyers argued, and came at a time of record-low border crossings. Trump and his administration have repeatedly claimed that the border is safer than ever, with CBP reporting border apprehensions 94% lower than they were during the Biden presidency, and Border Patrol “encounters” hitting their lowest levels in more than 50 years . The Nation underscored these figures as evidence that a wall is unnecessary. The tribe’s interim chief of police, James Cook, claimed there had been a 90% drop in reports of illegal entry over the preceding year, saying in a sworn declaration that smuggling and other border-related crimes had “almost disappeared.” Benjamin S. Hollinder, a senior Border Patrol official, argued in a sworn declaration opposing the tribe’s lawsuit that the absence of a wall on the Nation has produced a funneling effect, channeling smugglers onto the reservation, and saying that dynamic would intensify once the rest of Arizona was walled off. “Not having a border barrier system in this particular area makes it a vulnerable and a desirable area for [transnational criminal organizations] to operate,” wrote Hollinder. “If encounters of aliens entering illegally between ports of entry increase, vulnerabilities in the area will become particularly problematic.” The Nation sought the preliminary injunction to bar border wall activity until the litigation was resolved. On the eve of a July 22 hearing, DHS filed a notice affirming that to accelerate the project, it was waiving, in whole or in part, more than 30 laws, including several that mandate tribal consultation. In court filings, the government acknowledged its long history of working “cooperatively” with the tribal government while also arguing that the Nation “does not hold veto power over the United States’ sovereign duty to secure its borders.” Trump administration attorneys contended that an injunction was premature; planning was ongoing, thus problems the Nation envisioned could still be addressed. The government insisted construction would be limited to the Roosevelt Reservation, a 60-foot-wide zone that runs across California, Arizona and New Mexico on the U.S. side of the border, where CBP was authorized to construct barriers as it saw fit. Riyaz Kanji, the tribe’s lead attorney, argued the Roosevelt Reservation doesn’t extend onto tribal land, and even if it did the rugged landscape would force construction to diverge far from the 60-foot boundary. Sweeping as its powers were, Kanji contended, DHS could not override a sovereign government. The administration’s plans, he argued, constituted a “blatant and unprecedented disregard for the tribe’s rights.” Adam R.F. Gustafson, a Justice Department attorney, countered that the tribe had already approved a barrier on its land many years ago. The question now was what kind of barrier it should be. That was for DHS to decide, he argued. The department was “committed” to consultation, he continued. “We take very seriously the tribe’s views on this,” he told the court. The judge appeared swayed by DHS’ assurances but needed time to consider. “I don’t think the government is trying to go outside of that 60-foot strip,” he said. Signs placed by Tohono O’odham tribal leaders warn contractors that their presence on the reservation would be considered trespassing. Cam Mackey The O’odham suspected the government would not be as mindful as it claimed. Two days after the meeting with Mullin, the DHS secretary, a border wall contractor had “inadvertently disturbed a cultural site” west of the reservation. The crew had bulldozed a 70-foot swath through the Las Playas Intaglio, a 200-foot long earthen etching in the shape of a fish that was at least 6,500 years old . The site was well marked and well known to area archaeologists. Wynona P. Larson Yazzie, an O’odham tribal elder, Marine Corps veteran and former tribal police officer, had organized prayer runs that included stops at the intaglio. She’d visited the site the day before its destruction. Since then, she’d closely followed the Nation’s lawsuit. On Aug. 6, Larson Yazzie saw a disturbing filing from the tribe’s attorneys. They’d received word that in four days government contractors would enter the reservation to conduct tests. DHS, the tribe argued, was “exploiting” the judge’s reflection period to “move forward with highly disputed actions.” Tribal leaders erected dozens of 8-foot-wide “no trespassing” signs along the three main access roads leading through the reservation to the border. Larson Yazzie, meanwhile, began making plans of her own. She was joined by Amy Juan, a longtime O’odham activist. Juan, 40, had grown up riding in her grandfather’s truck over the clanking cattle guard at Ko:li Ki:jig, a traditional crossing on the U.S.-Mexico line. After 9/11, a locking gate was placed over the cattle guard. The Border Patrol built a “forward operating base” near her grandparents’ home that would eventually feature a helipad, a detention space and an endless cycle of agents. Around the reservation’s perimeter, CBP established some of the largest Border Patrol stations in the country. Checkpoints went up on roads leading north. O’odham tribal members Daniel Oriol Figueroa Cervantes, left, from Mexico, and Amy Juan, from Arizona, visit over the border barrier at the Tadai Me:i prayer camp on Aug. 29. Ryan Devereaux/ProPublica Human rights groups documented U.S.-born tribal members being arrested and deported, and verbal and physical abuse by Border Patrol agents. CBP did not respond when asked about the report’s allegations. For Juan, the Nation’s collaboration with DHS had sacrificed safety and civil liberties for elusive gains. Virtually everyone on the reservation had been touched by the dark side of border smuggling. During the mid-2000s, some tribal members, enticed by a chance at life-changing money, got involved in moving people and drugs, fueling cycles of arrest and incarceration that exacerbated challenges the community was already facing. At the same time, virtually everyone also had a story about negative interactions with the Border Patrol — a child traumatized at a checkpoint, an unlawful traffic stop or a loved one assaulted by an agent. “We want safety and the same respect as the next person,” Juan said. “We’ve never been against keeping people safe, but at what cost?” Larson Yazzie was similarly concerned. She worried that in the face of DHS pressure the Nation would fold and, like the intaglio, the borderlands would be lost. A tribal member stands near the fire burning in the Tadai Me:i prayer camp in early September. Cam Mackey Prayer fires are an important O’odham tradition, often convened in moments of communal struggle. To Larson Yazzie, the coming of a wall was such a time. The chosen site was symbolic: the border gate at Ko:li Ki:jig. The camp had limited amenities — cots and chairs that encircled the fire, a cooler for ice, a weathered canopy for relief from the sun. They called it Tadai Me:i — roadrunner on fire. Someone was always awake to watch the flame, which was lit on Aug. 9, as the Trump administration’s contractors were preparing to enter the reservation. The first drone sighting in the area was recorded the following night, at 11:43 p.m., documented in the first of two activity logs. Kept in spiral notebooks, the logs offered a minute-by-minute account of what participants in the ceremony saw and heard. The handwritten observations, shared with ProPublica, span 13 days and chart a steady escalation by DHS, culminating in an elite tactical team that blocked tribal authorities from issuing trespassing citations to contractors or removing them. The camp wasn’t a protest site like those seen in Minneapolis, Chicago or other cities over the past year. Participants didn’t shout at passing Border Patrol agents. They focused on the fire, making sure there was enough sugai — creosote bush, a fragrant desert plant — to keep it burning. They were in ceremony, concentrating on morning prayers and nightly cleanses. The atmosphere was that of a family gathering in a moment of crisis. There were jokes and levity amid the uncertainty. Larson Yazzie knew at least one legislative council member who opposed the gathering. They feared it could lead to large groups converging on the reservation to physically block the border wall, in an occupation similar to the 10-month protest on Standing Rock Sioux land that halted construction of the Dakota Access Pipeline in 2016. The idea terrified tribal leaders. With its lethal heat and unforgiving terrain, the desert was dangerous enough without outsiders squaring off against Border Patrol. A ceremonial fire burns on Aug. 27 at a prayer camp near the traditional Ko:li Ki:jig border crossing on the Tohono O’odham Nation. Nate Sosa Supporters of the ceremonial fire were themselves uneasy. They knew the story of Ray Mattia , the 58-year-old who was shot and killed by the Border Patrol in 2023 while unarmed on the doorstep of his home on the reservation. Agents, who were backing tribal police on the call, claimed to have mistaken a cellphone he was holding for a gun. “My fear is that they gonna start shooting us,” said 24-year-old camp visitor Collin Quasule. Quasule had videos on his phone of recent interactions he’d had with federal agents, including agents trailing him as he drove around the reservation, following him to his home, pulling him over without explaining why, refusing to accept his legal name and birthdate, and winking at him when he protested his detention. Across the reservation, community members were on the lookout for large trucks traveling together with out-of-state plates. On Aug. 12, Juan received a call about a caravan: six trucks with Texas plates, following an unmarked SUV with government plates. She called the tribe’s police department. The caravan was intercepted and escorted off the land by tribal authorities. The driver of the unmarked vehicle was confirmed to be a Border Patrol agent. The interception was one of nearly a dozen tribal police recorded over a three-day period. During the camp’s first seven days, the activity log filled with nearly 665 observations, mostly federal agents buzzing around their location. An activity log kept by tribal members documents border wall construction and law enforcement activity on the Tohono O’odham Nation. Ryan Devereaux/ProPublica While many would drive by without stopping, other agents would park and watch. At least one was reported snapping photos of the campers. ProPublica later obtained video of an agent doing exactly that. Mexican security forces, both military and police, were also observed conversing with Border Patrol agents over the international boundary. “It appeared that the 2 BPs were showing the Mexicans pictures on their phones,” read an Aug. 11 entry. “Surveillance has heightened,” Juan said, days after the prayer fire was lit. “Drones, helicopters, a lot of air activity.” The choppers included both marked CBP and what appeared to be military Black Hawks. The drones were of the handheld quadcopter variety, let loose directly over the camp, at times during prayer song ceremonies. On the fourth night, a gathering was held. Upwards of 100 people turned up, including members of distant sister tribes. The evening was peaceful until Juan received a text from an elder couple who’d left early to return to their home near Tucson. The Border Patrol had stopped them at a checkpoint a half-mile outside the reservation, they reported. The officers said they were conducting an “immigration check” and asked to see tribal ID. “Where you guys coming from?” the agent asked. “Ceremony,” the couple replied. “Oh,” the agent said, “is that the one going on down south?” The encounter was unusual, said Juan. The checkpoint is rarely staffed. When agents are on hand, she said, “they never ask us for a tribal ID.” When Juan shared the information with the gathering, people immediately began packing up, afraid, she surmised, of a late-night encounter with Border Patrol. A Border Patrol agent stops to film the Tadai Me:i prayer camp on Sept. 30. Davy Cross On Aug. 14, Judge Richard J. Leon declined the Nation’s injunction request. “I fully expect the government in the months ahead to follow through on its guarantees of consultation and cooperation with the Nation to address the Nation’s concerns regarding border wall construction!” he wrote. Eleven days later, on Aug. 25, the Border Patrol sent the Nation its one-minute notice that the contractors were coming. Larson Yazzie jumped in her truck and raced for the border to document what was happening. An agent on foot stopped her. He’d laid a spike strip in the road ahead, he warned. Larson Yazzie filmed the contractors in the distance. When the tribal police department’s interim chief arrived, he too was stopped at a Border Patrol roadblock. A trio of Border Patrol supervisors approached, including two from a nearby station and a third representing BORTAC, the agency’s special operations wing. The SWAT-style agents wore desert camo, masks and patterned scarves favored by U.S. military units in Iraq and Afghanistan. It was only after promising not to interfere that the tribal police chief was permitted to record. He observed three drilling rigs manned by a handful of operators. An equal number of agents stood guard. The contractors’ heavy vehicles were all beyond the 60-foot zone that government attorneys assured the judge they would not leave. The chief also encountered a trio of Bureau of Indian Affairs agents, who claimed to have been sent on orders from Washington, D.C. Their mission, they said, was to “preserve the peace and monitor activities.” A Border Patrol vehicle is parked near the Tadai Me:i prayer camp on the Tohono O’odham Nation. Cam Mackey For the prayer camp’s participants, the need to relight the flame, which they had extinguished after a seven-day ceremony, was self-evident. They began that night. Davy Cross, a stocky 57-year-old with an intricate tattoo running down the left side of his face, was tending the fire when, at 4:33 a.m., he noticed buzzing above his head. At first, the machines were visible. There were at least five. “I seen all the red lights,” Cross recalled. But as they got lower, the drones went dark. Cross could still hear them and feel the draft of the rotors against his skin. Then, he said, “they disappeared.” The drones were soon replaced by an airplane and a helicopter. Shortly after 9 a.m., a caravan of Border Patrol and construction vehicles trundled into view. The work trucks continued on, but much of the Border Patrol force remained, forming a semicircle around the camp with Mexican state police closing the loop on the other side of the line. “We got surround[ed] by over 30 vehicles,” Cross wrote in the activity log. A video of the moment spread across social media in the borderlands. The tribe’s attorneys filed an appeal of the judge’s order allowing construction to proceed and pleaded for a halt to the government’s activities. They argued that the Trump administration was making “a mockery” of the court’s expectation of “consultation and cooperation.” A convoy of Border Patrol and construction vehicles pass the Tadai Me:i prayer camp on Aug. 29. Ryan Devereaux/ProPublica That night at the camp, Larson Yazzie was singing prayer songs when Juan pulled in. It was near midnight. Border Patrol agents were coming and going constantly. Some passed without stopping. Others idled at the edge of the firelight while the red lights of a surveillance blimp blinked over the mountains to the east. Tadai Me:i wasn’t the only pocket of resistance on the border. In Texas, the Trump administration’s plans to run a wall through Big Bend National Park had brought together an unusual coalition that saw environmental nonprofits and river guides standing with hunters , ranchers and local sheriffs in opposition to the project. One week before the armed convoy rolled onto the Tohono O’odham reservation, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott announced that after speaking with the secretary of DHS, he’d secured a pause on the controversial project. “There are technology tools that don’t include barriers,” the governor said at a press conference. “Think of drones, think of fiber optics.” Last week, a judge granted a preliminary injunction halting construction in the Big Bend area while a lawsuit against the project proceeds. To Juan, it was darkly ironic. For two and a half decades, the Nation had been a laboratory for the technology Abbott described. Yet when tribal leaders made that case, they were told to stand down; the wall was coming whether they accepted it or not. “What makes Texas the exception to us is very clear,” Juan said. “It’s good old boy conversations that are happening between the politicians and the CBP commissioners and Markwayne Mullin.” Sunrise at Tadai Me:i prayer camp on Sept. 26 Ryan Devereaux/ProPublica The early fire watch that morning fell to a young Pascua Yaqui member named Nate Sosa. At 3:28 a.m., Sosa heard a noise — a round being chambered in a weapon. A Border Patrol agent had exited his vehicle. With a long gun slung low across his back, he shined a light into Mexico. He then walked within feet of the campers asleep on their cots. A half an hour later, a drone flew in from the north, followed by a helicopter. After that came a convoy dozens of vehicles long. At 6:02, while Larson Yazzie was leading the camp in prayer, a helicopter passed overhead. An hour later, a drone ascended above the fire. Liz Quiroga, a 28-year-old tribal member and regular at the prayer site, sat with the camp’s logbook open in her lap. Over the next five days, the book would fill with 379 observations. Nearly two-thirds involved Border Patrol units near the fire. The arrival of Mexican authorities was documented six times. An additional 39 entries referenced unmarked vehicles and suspected “undercovers.” Whether those individuals were Border Patrol, contractors or tribal police was unclear. The logbook cataloged a dozen instances of aircraft flying over the camp, including four helicopters, three planes and five drones. “Nobody has any idea what’s actually happening out here,” Quiroga said. “This is true dystopia.” While its legal challenge continues, the Nation has ceased attempting to remove border wall contractors from its lands. The camp and the surveillance that’s come with it remain.
articles.summary: As construction on former President Trump's border wall nears completion, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is intensifying its surveillance and enforcement activities against a border tribe. Reports detail the use of advanced surveillance technology, masked agents, and drones, creating an atmosphere of intimidation. This aggressive posture raises serious human rights concerns, highlights the militarization of border zones, and underscores the impact of federal policy on indigenous sovereignty.

articles.title: Congress Debates Social Media Ban for Under-18s
articles.content: Why Congress should think twice about banning under-18s from social media Oct 10, 2026 2:00 PM PHT Gelo Gonzales Listen to this article Powered by  Speechify Already have Rappler+? Sign in to listen to groundbreaking journalism. SOCIAL MEDIA. TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, Snapchat, X, Reddit app icons are seen in this illustration taken June 15, 2026 Dado Ruvic/Reuters INFO Australia's experience and a more nuanced House proposal raise questions about the effectiveness, proportionality, and unintended consequences of a blanket social media ban AT A GLANCE Philippine lawmakers are debating a proposed ban on social media access for individuals under 18, amid concerns about online dangers such as cyberbullying and exploitation. Australia's experience with a similar age restriction shows that bans may not effectively reduce social media use among minors, highlighting challenges in enforcement and the need to address harmful platform features. The House of Representatives has proposed a more nuanced approach, allowing restricted access for older teenagers while banning social media for those 13 and younger, emphasizing the importance of digital literacy and the need for targeted regulations. This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors . MANILA, Philippines – Protecting children from the dangers of social media is an increasingly urgent concern for governments worldwide. But does keeping young people off these platforms necessarily make them safer? This is a question Philippine lawmakers must confront as Congress deliberates on legislation prohibiting anyone below 18 from accessing social media and other high-risk digital services. On Thursday, October 8, the Senate approved Senate Bill No. 2424 , or the Safe Media Access and Responsible Technology for Kids in Digital Spaces (SMART KIDS) Act, by a vote of 16-1. The measure comes amid concerns about cyberbullying, online sexual exploitation, violent content, grooming and manipulation, and addictive algorithms. But an outright ban covering everyone under 18 — the widest-reaching age threshold in the world if enacted — is arguably a draconian response to a serious problem. It raises questions about proportionality, enforcement, and whether restricting access addresses the underlying causes of online harm, or just delays regulation that deals with the addictive and harmful features of social media platform. Australia implemented a nationwide social media minimum-age restriction in December 2025, prohibiting those under 16 from holding accounts on covered platforms. Its experience offers lessons for Philippine lawmakers: implementing it is a challenging matter. According to Australia’s eSafety Commissioner , social media usage among children under 16 only declined from 85.9% before the restrictions to 81.5% three months after. In other words, roughly eight in ten children continued using social media despite the ban. A CNA Talking Point documentary showed teenagers circumventing age-verification measures. Some passed facial age-estimation checks because the technology incorrectly identified them as older than 16. Conversely, some adults were denied access after being mistakenly classified as minors. Teenagers also described creating new accounts, using alternative devices, and seeking help from adults. An expert involved in Australia’s age-assurance technology trial attributed some failures to inconsistent implementation by platforms. Australia’s experience illustrates the limitations of what may be a stopgap measure, particularly when enforcement remains inconsistent. If young people can readily circumvent restrictions, how much protection does the law actually provide? A blanket ban doesn’t address the harmful platform features, including algorithms that amplify disturbing content, infinite scrolling, autoplay, and notifications designed to keep users engaged. Such features do not disappear when minors are prohibited from accessing platforms. Ian Russell, a British online safety campaigner whose 14-year-old daughter Molly died by suicide in 2017, has questioned blanket restrictions. An inquest concluded that harmful online content contributed to Molly’s death. Despite campaigning for stronger protections, Russell argued in a BBC Newscast interview that banning children does not address the source of harm , and believes governments should hold technology companies accountable for algorithms and design features that expose users to dangerous content. Restrictions and more targeted regulation against dangerous features are not mutually exclusive. But we must recognize what the proposal of a ban for under-18s: a stopgap solution that doesn’t go at the root of the issue. The Senate raised the age threshold from the original under-16 proposal to under 18. The increase comes amid recent school shootings and other violent incidents involving young people in the Philippines. But lawmakers must establish whether sufficient evidence connects these incidents to social media and whether a blanket ban would prevent similar tragedies. A policy driven primarily by fear rather than scientific evidence risks unintended consequences. This concern is central to Senator Risa Hontiveros’ dissenting vote. “Eighteen is the legal threshold for adulthood. But it is certainly not a developmental threshold,” Hontiveros said. She argued that a 13-year-old and a 17-year-old are not developmentally equivalent simply because both are minors. Hontiveros cited the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, which recognizes children’s evolving capacities as they mature. She also emphasized that social media provides livelihoods through online selling and content creation, helps children connect with OFW parents, and allows them to report abuse and participate in public discussions. At 15, Filipinos can already vote in Sangguniang Kabataan elections and legally work, subject to labor regulations. Yet the proposed ban would restrict access to platforms used for political participation and economic opportunities. Beyond these consequences, a blanket ban could also be viewed as a repressive restriction on young people’s freedom of expression. Digital platforms have become common avenues for teenagers to voice opinions, exchange ideas, and participate in public discourse. The House of Representatives has taken a different approach. On October 6, it approved on second reading House Bill No. 11566, or the Safe and Friendly Environment for Kids in Digital Spaces Act. According to INQUIRER.net , the House measure proposes a complete social media ban for children 13 and younger, while allowing older teenagers restricted access. The legislation would shield teenagers from harmful advertising, livestreaming, algorithm-driven short-video feeds, and gambling-like mechanisms. It would also restrict contact with unknown adults and certain artificial intelligence features. Pasig Representative Roman Romulo, who sponsored the measure, said the distinction was deliberate. “Younger children require a clear minimum age boundary, while adolescents require a framework that recognizes their growing capacity for independence without disregarding the risks to which they remain exposed,” Romulo said. The House approach resembles the age-appropriate framework advocated by Hontiveros, recognizing that older teenagers can gain greater independence while retaining safeguards. A blanket ban could also undermine digital literacy. Young people need to understand algorithms, misinformation, online predators, scams, and exploitation. Would an 18-year-old encountering social media for the first time necessarily be better equipped than a younger teenager who gradually learned under parental guidance? Supporters may argue that digital literacy can be taught without social media access. But supervised exposure offers another approach. Social media companies have also advocated age-appropriate frameworks, including teen accounts and parental controls. Their position warrants scrutiny, given their commercial incentives to retain users. Again, governments could instead impose enforceable standards addressing harmful algorithms, addictive design, and inadequate child protections. As the House reviews SB 2424, it has an opportunity to examine which restrictions are proportionate, enforceable, and supported by evidence. The goal should not simply be to keep children off social media, but to make the digital environments they encounter safer. – Rappler.com Must Read Against oppressive algorithms, addictive design, parents can’t always keep up Dig Deeper Add to Preferred Sources Share in Chat Facebook X (Twitter) Copy Link Related Topics Facebook Instagram investigations on tech companies Meta Platforms social media Twitter Gelo Gonzales @gelogonzales86 Gelo Gonzales is Rappler’s technology editor. articles.content: 본문 글로벌워치 “한국, AI 인프라 최적의 파트너”…실리콘밸리 VC 거물 a16z, 국내 기업과 맞손 선담은 기자 수정 2026-10-12 11:01 펼침 0:00 Your browser does not support the audio element. 앤드리슨 호로위츠, 이번 주 방한해 국내 기업 연쇄 미팅 실리콘밸리 대표 벤처캐피털(VC) 앤드리슨 호로위츠(a16z). 실리콘밸리 대표 벤처캐피털(VC) 앤드리슨 호로위츠(a16z)가 한국을 찾아 국내 인공지능(AI)·반도체 기업과 협력 기회 모색에 나선다. 12일 업계에 따르면, a16z 인프라 투자팀은 이번주 한국을 방문해 국내 인공지능 하드웨어·인프라 기업 및 관계자들과 만나 기술 개발 등 사업 협력 방안을 논의한다. a16z는 지난 7월 이재명 대통령이 참석한 ‘실리콘밸리 벤처투자 밋업(교류 모임)’에서 국민연금공단과 양해각서(MOU)를 체결한 6개 벤처캐피털 중 하나다. 이번 방한은 a16z가 지난달 11억달러(약 1조5000억원) 규모로 조성한 ‘머신 에이지 펀드’의 투자처를 발굴하기 위한 행보로 풀이된다. 이 펀드는 반도체·컴퓨팅·메모리·네트워크 등 하드웨어는 물론 전력·냉각·데이터센터를 아우르는 인공지능 인프라 전반을 투자 대상으로 삼는다. a16z는 세계 최고 수준의 제조 역량을 갖춘 한국의 반도체와 로보틱스 산업을 핵심 협력 분야로 주목하고 있다. 앞서 a16z는 지난해 말 박성모 아시아태평양(APAC) 사업개발 총괄을 국내 첫 인력으로 영입하며 크립토 생태계와의 협력을 추진해왔다. 최근에는 인공지능을 비롯한 국내 기술 생태계 전반으로 협력 관계를 확대 중이다. 라구 라구람 a16z 제너럴 파트너는 “인공지능의 발전은 소프트웨어뿐 아니라 기술 인프라 전반을 빠르게 변화시키고 있다”며 “한국은 반도체와 로보틱스 등 핵심 분야에서 세계적인 기술력과 탄탄한 산업 기반을 갖추고 있는 만큼 이번 방문을 통해 한국 기업 및 산업 관계자들과 직접 만나 새로운 기술과 사업 기회에 대해 폭넓게 논의할 수 있기를 기대한다”고 말했다. 2009년 마크 앤드리슨과 벤 호로위츠가 공동 설립한 a16z는 오픈에이아이(AI), 스페이스엑스(X), 에어비앤비, 피그마, 코인베이스, 커서(Cursor) 등에 투자한 세계 최대 테크 전문 벤처캐피털이다. 선담은 기자 sun@hani.co.kr

articles.title: France School Protests Go Deeper Than Rioting
articles.content: Student protests in France are an expression of the country’s deep political and economic crisis, says Jan Rovný, a Czech professor at Paris’s Sciences Po. Students from elite schools and universities have joined secondary-school pupils from deprived suburbs in protesting for education reforms. Rovný explains how these young people protest in solidarity with less fortunate peers, invoking ideals of equality embedded in French minds. He explained how traditionally violent protests in the republic are often met by disproportionately heavy-handed policing. The French government has tried to hide students’ dissatisfaction by blaming far-left groups. What do the protests say about French society? Are they a revolt by young people against poor conditions or part of broader woes? It is important to realise that the situation in France does not concern only young people and education, it goes deeper than that. The era of French president Emmanuel Macron is coming to an end. For several years now, the country has been run by unstable minority governments, which all face one key problem: how to draft a budget, unveiled on October 1, and push it through parliament. It is clear that the country is in a very difficult economic situation , because its debt stands at around 117 percent of GDP. The interest rate is rising and approaching five percent. Every day, newspapers write that France cannot bear this burden. French society is realising that it is at an impasse both politically and economically, that the current elite has no answer, and that savings must be made in various areas. People from many sectors are now speaking out to say they do not want cuts. Or that they have problems that are not being addressed. And young people have a clear view of this, and that is why they are mobilising. The protest began with specific demands from secondary-school pupils, who clearly identified shortcomings in education — notably missing teachers, overcrowded classrooms and schools in poor condition, some with rats running around and no running water. Yet the protest quickly grew into a nationwide movement. Why have these particular issues proved so powerful? Partly because they underscore this whole situation, and partly because this is a young generation that represents France’s future. Young people are protesting to say: look at the future we are facing. And parents and teachers largely agree with them. The protests began in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis and did not arise as a result of a new government reform, but from the everyday experiences of students. What does this tell us about how young French people view the state and its ability to provide public education? France generally has relatively low trust in political institutions. Young people tend to feel this even more strongly, because they are generally less politically engaged and therefore feel they are, in some way, discriminated against. They see the state as failing to care sufficiently for them and unable to cope. This is compounded by the approaching elections. We know that the current government is fragile, and we also know that society, as well as the political establishment as a whole, is deeply polarised, with the extremist camps in particular set to enter the elections strengthened. Staying with the protests, it is interesting that private secondary schools have joined state schools. On Tuesday, the French daily Le Monde showed protests outisde Paris Lycée Henri-IV attended by children from elite families - and where Macron studied. How do you explain the involvement of private schools unlikely to experience the same problems as public ones? Exactly. That is my situation as well. I teach at a very prestigious university with a beautiful campus a short distance from the Louvre. Yet our students are protesting. They are protesting because they recognise that French society has major inequalities affecting young people in suburbs like Saint-Denis or Val-de-Marne where conditions are worse. Better off students are mobilising in solidarity - the concept of equality has been part of France’s political consciousness since the French Revolution . Those privately educated pupil therefore see it as their duty to join protests even though they enjoy far better conditions. France is described as a strong state where education is regarded as a public service and a fundamental pillar of the French Republic. Could frustration over lack of basic conditions in schools be a reason for current anger? Of course, and it has several dimensions. The French Third Republic was based on the idea that public education was the means through which modern citizens are created. State schools, established by law at the time, were seen as a fundamental pillar of the new, young democracy. When you walk around Paris or anywhere else in France, you notice that every school has both the French and European flags above its entrance, along with the words “liberty, equality, fraternity” — the motto of the republicand revolution. Historically, schools drew children out of traditional families, which at that time were highly Catholic, and turned them into modern citizens. That is the country's foundation. Another factor is that the French state is very powerful: public spending accounts for more than 50% of GDP. The state is hierarchical, yet it seeks to show that it can do everything, including providing schooling for all. That position is increasingly hard to defend, particularly when money is short and public spending must be cut. France has a long history of street protests. Is the current situation different in any way from previous social conflicts? It is difficult to say. What is interesting is that secondary-school students are mobilising. That is relatively unusual, though not entirely unprecedented. It has happened in the past too, but was less visible. Teachers’ unions are now joining these students, as are broader trade unions and public-sector employees generally. University students are also already on strike. There is talk that farmers could join them. It may gather momentum and, as with the yellow vest protests , everyone who criticises the government may take to the streets. That is essentially the majority. What is interesting about the current protests is that they are led by underage young people who are not yet able to vote, yet can still place the government under enormous pressure. How do you explain this? They are young and have the time and ability to mobilise. They are able to sustain it and have their own internal organisation. Certain political forces, primarily from the far left, are helping or supporting them, but only to a limited extent. I think the protest is genuinely organic, rather than being directed by a political party or political agitators. Protester holds a placard reading 'Education is a right, not a privilege'. Source: EPA/Firas Abdullah. Young people feel they have something to say, and they can mobilise with the support of some teachers, some parents and now also broader sections of society — both university students and some trade union organisations. It may last for some time. The French government may fear protesting young people more than other protest groups. Why do protesting young people carry such particular political weight in France? It is probably a memory of 1968 when student mobilisation shifted the entire country to open up certain issues. Sudents are able to mobilise and persevere because they do not lose income when they strike, whereas workers who go on strike do not receive pay for those days, which can be a serious problem for some. There is also a significance of young people being the future, who say: no, we simply want this country to be different, because it will be ours and we will be responsible for it when you are no longer here. On Monday, a 15-year-old boy lost his hand after a police grenade exploded, with several other injuries caused by police being investigated. Could this fundamentally change the public mood? Protests in France tend to be more violent than others are used to. I think it works both ways. I am convinced that the overwhelming majority of protesting students are peaceful, but some people with somewhat different intentions join them. They are called 'casseurs' (wreckers)who simply exploit the situation to throw stones at police or set bins on fire. On the other side are the police, who can become highly aggressive quickly. There is now a major debate over whether the police response is proportionate. These responses divide the left and the right quite clearly with the government and the right wing supporting police, while the left argues that police brutality is pervasive. It is quite shocking to see footage of armed police officers beating children in the street. Exactly. And the police will have to be careful not to lose control of the situation. The response of the education minister, who has told students that he will listen to them, is also interesting. The interior minister and the prime minister have instead responded that the police are doing their job and that the interventions are proportionate. The government is blaming radical left-wing groups for the violence, accusing the far-left party La France Insoumise ( France Unbowed) of inciting riots. Do you find this political explanation convincing, or does it take attention away from students’ genuine demands? It is difficult to say. I would not be at all surprised if extremist groups of any kind joined the protests, although left-wing groups are probably more likely. It is difficult to speculate on the extent to which this is directed from the leadership of France Unbowed. However, I do not think it is to any great extent. Representatives of this left-wing party, including its MPs and local politicians, joined student, thereby legitimising these protests. But I very much doubt that the party would seek to organise greater violence in order to draw attention to the situation. That suggestion seems somewhat extreme to me. France is only a few months away from presidential elections. Could this discontent become one of the issues in the election campaign? Everyone is trying to gain political advantage from it in some way. It is quite clear that the typical Jean-Luc Mélenchon voter supports the students and government criticism more generally. Ordinary citizens do not want to see violence or rubbish being set on fire, and this sentiment is probably much stronger on the right, which automatically sees Mélenchon as an instigator of unrest. Mélenchon needs to be careful. To win a larger number of voters, he must also appear as someone who is trying to prevent violence. That is what he attempted to do. A few days ago, he addressed students, saying: mobilise, but your actions must be non-violent. He specifically added that they must be disciplined. In your view, what could be the boiling point at which governments will no longer be able to calm the situation through promises or concessions? That is a difficult question. These protests cannot go on forever, since many students realise what they want is better teaching conditions, so that they can prepare better for the baccalaureate examinations, which are approaching in the spring for those in their final year. So they may want to sit down and study. If the government manages to offer at least some concrete solutions to the fundamental problems — above all, on timetables and teacher allocation on lycées — it may calm the situation. If it does not, I do not know. Can we therefore understand the current protests as an expression of a crisis in French society, or as evidence that some form of civic mobilisation and the belief that protest can change something still function in France? It is both. From young people’s perspective, the positive aspect is that they are able to mobilise, take their future into their own hands and say: this is a problem. We told you this, you did not listen to us, so now we are changing tactics and will protest visibly. I think that is fundamentally positive — without the violence. On the other hand, French society is in deep crisis, and overcoming it will require an explicit change in the narrative - a change in the system. There will need to be some recognition that France is no longer what it used to be; while it remains one of the larger countries of the EU, it is now more or less an ordinary country and it must behave accordingly and see itself in that way. Understanding this is quite difficult, and it will certainly require political courage and a political figure capable of turning frustrations into something positive. Jan Rovný (1978) is professor of political science at the Centre for European Studies and Comparative Politics at Sciences Po university in Paris. His academic specialisms include political competition in Europe, ideological conflict and voter behaviour. He studied at McGill University in Montreal, Canada, at the the College of Europe in Bruges, and at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden. Unlock article and share

articles.title: Fingerprints Are the New Cookies for Tracking
articles.content: You're protected from the methods I use here. You disabled JavaScript, so this fingerprinting trick can't run at all. You're still vulnerable to network-based methods. Read on to see what it does to everyone else. From now on I’ll call you: … computing… Try refreshing the page. Clear the cookies. Connect to a VPN. You’re still the … . Now open it on your phone or some other device and your nickname will be different and just as consistent. Is it different in incognito? Good. But it’s always the same? Bad news. Imagine this: Most websites you visit get paid to show ads and indirectly run my script that lets me know you’re the … . I can use it to decide what ads you’ll see. But more importantly, if you’ve made an account on that website, I can offer to buy your data - whatever they can share under their privacy policy: your name, activity, conversations with AI… Pretty soon I’d know more about you than your friends do - perhaps more than you know yourself. “So what?” - you say. “I have nothing to hide. And I prefer my ads to be relevant… sometimes they show me exactly what I need! And the data is anonymised anyway…” See, the thing is, it’s not about you at all. It’s not really about the ads anymore either. Nobody cares about you. And if the police or your government happen to care, I’ll gladly take their money too. I look at all this data and I don’t see people. I see patterns. Patterns emerging out of patterns. A living, digital fractal state of the economy, society and human psyche. The crystal ball of the 21st century and it’s made of silicon! That’s the product. And to the highest bidder it goes! What does that make you then? A gear? An ox? A volunteer? Fingerprints are the new cookies Remember the big fuss about third-party cookies? It was so big that the EU had already rolled out one of its greatest inventions - consent banners. If EU ships faster than tech companies, that can only mean the tech companies are sitting on their hands. And one of those tech companies happens to hold two-thirds of the browser market. What was the play? Let’s give it up for Google - the biggest ad company on Earth! ACT I. PRESSURE - “PRIVACY IS PARAMOUNT TO US, IN EVERYTHING WE DO.” It’s 2019 and the cookies are still hot. It’s become bad PR and Safari and Firefox already block them. A year later Google pledges: we will destroy cookies!! And establish a new, privacy-first reign. ACT II. DISTRACTION - “INSTEAD OF DEPRECATING THIRD-PARTY COOKIES, WE WOULD INTRODUCE A NEW EXPERIENCE” 5 years later: people are now preoccupied with far greater worries than cookies, and the solutions Google has developed (Privacy Sandbox) kinda suck and have raised antitrust concerns so nobody uses them. “You know what, let’s just keep the cookies. We’ll mask your IP address* though!” (* but only when incognito while authenticated) (** in the end they didn’t even deliver on that) ACT III. ACCELERATION - YOU CAN NOW USE DEVICE FINGERPRINTING IN OUR AD PRODUCTS Now there’s a better way to know who’s who! How does fingerprinting work? Nice, let’s nerd out properly. You visit a website. Your browser sends a request to the server and the server returns code for the browser to run. The request already reveals information about you; what browser you use, the language it’s in, the OS that runs it and your IP address, which the server needs to send you the response. That often reveals your location. Then the code runs. See, we’ve made a lot of civilizational progress in making browsing safe. Long gone are the days when getting a virus just by visiting a website was a daily concern . The thing is, the definition of safety varies depending on who you ask. The broad consensus ends at isolation: a website’s code can’t see the data stored by other websites, and it can’t see your files or other applications without permission. Chrome and Edge stop here. Then you have Safari (especially on iOS/macOS 26+) and Firefox extending that definition to privacy, but they still don’t fully protect you from fingerprinting. Brave and Tor are the leading privacy-first browsers, with up and coming Mullvad Browser (Mullvad being, in my opinion, one of the best VPN providers out there). The code runs on your hardware, which can be measured in ways that produce consistent and unique readings. There’s not much that can be done about this really, so there’s only two established solutions: feed a little bit of noise here and there. It’s called farbling and that’s what Brave does to make your fingerprint inconsistent. make everything look the same, always, so there’s no telling browser users apart. Tor and Mullvad adopt this approach. Ok, let’s create a fingerprint So there are two sources for data that can make up your fingerprint; the network request and the code environment. When you look at network, the data is generally either fragile or generic: the IP address; in a ‘happy path’ where one person always uses the same IP address, it might be the only data you need. But commonly people do a lot of browsing on mobile networks, they share the WiFi with others, they use VPNs or their home network’s IP address is rotated by the ISP. It’s fragile as such. headers like User-Agent or Accept-Language ; reveal your browser, OS, versions and the language set. When you can execute code on the device, you have ways to measure its hardware qualities (without any permission prompts!) and these are surprisingly stable: GPU; behaviour, vendor, driver CPU; behaviour, vendor, number of threads memory size display data; resolution, pixel ratio, refresh rate audio processing device model And on the software level; installed fonts, extensions, system info… Millions of devices use the latest Chrome, there are millions of Macs with the M4 chip and there are millions of browsers in French. But when you look at devices that run the latest Chrome in French on an M4 , that number now drops significantly. Add to it hardware measurements and it gets so low it becomes practically unique. The fingerprint doesn’t need to be truly, globally unique - it just needs to be unique enough to tell people apart in your sample size. A ZIP code (inferred from IP), a birth date (you’ve given away on some platform) and sex (you fill it in everywhere) together are enough to uniquely identify over 60% of Americans. You can always add another variable to decrease the potential pool of candidates. Information Entropy Have you ever played Akinator ? You think of a character, a genie asks you some twenty questions, and somehow it knows. That’s fingerprinting in a nutshell, except your browser answers the questions for you. Once you understand information entropy, Akinator’s magic turns into a simple trick. Let’s simplify with that game where you have to guess the character on a board through questions like “Is my character a man?”. If I say “yes”, and half of the characters on your board are men, you’re now considering only half of the total candidates. Now we can say that my answer gave you log₂(100 / 50) = log₂(2) = 1 bit of information , because it cut the pool of candidates in half. The bits you get from one answer are called its surprisal: the rarer the answer, the more it tells you. a trait shared by 1 in 2 people is worth 1 bit (is a man), 1 in 8 is worth 3 bits (has a mustache), and 1 in 128 is worth 7 bits (has one eye). Surprisal quantifies the value of the answer, and entropy quantifies the value of the question. If 1 person in 128 is one-eyed, then asking about it will yield ‘no’ 127 times in 128. Answer Probability Surprisal Entropy contribution Yes 1/128 log₂(128 / 1) = 7 bits 1/128 x 7 = ~0.055 No 127/128 log₂(128 / 127) = ~0.0113 bits 127/128 x 0.0113 = ~0.011 Summing up the contribution of each possible answer, the question itself is worth ~0.066 bits of entropy - that’s the average amount of bits you gain from an answer. When we combine traits that are independent we simply add up their bits or multiply the ratios, so a man with a mustache and one eye would mean 11 bits, or 1 in 2048. Alas, as Thomas Bayes would have you know, nothing is ever so simple in practice. A mustache is already a strong indicator of a man, and a man is probably more likely to have one eye. The traits are not independent so the bits don’t really add up. Some interesting applications of this type of reasoning: In medical diagnostics : A positive result from a 99% accurate test for a disease known to affect 0.01% of the population is about 100 times more likely to be wrong than you are to have the disease. You need more evidence! In cryptography : A password made out of four random words is as strong as eight random keyboard characters (but much easier to remember!) In forensic science : singling out one person in a city of a million takes about 20 bits. A witness description that matches 1 person in 1,000 provides only 10 bits, which still leaves a thousand possible suspects. So what can I do about it? Test your browser: coveryourtracks.eff.org shows you how unique your fingerprint is, with entropy for each measured data point. If you’re using Chrome you’re basically walking around with an ID on your forehead. Safari and Firefox offer some level of protection, but you’re still identifiable by advanced trackers. Brave , Tor and Mullvad Browser are the only major browsers at the moment that implement advanced protections against fingerprinting. If you don’t feel like switching browsers, I get it. I am a big Arc fan myself and unfortunately it’s discontinued and will never have any privacy features. There are extensions like JShelter - they disrupt fingerprinting scripts by intercepting browser API calls. But they also break some websites. Same problem applies to Firefox’s Resist Fingerprinting feature. The ironic truth is, privacy extensions make you more unique, since fewer people have them. So a smart tracker could detect that, ignore the signals disrupted by the extension and focus on the ones that are not. No extension can be as effective as engine-level protection built into the browser. So if you don’t want to be tracked, you gotta commit. methods used on this page I’m simply creating a hash out of a few measurements of your device. Any of these change and the hash is now different. articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox Trump said he considered the advertisements to be a “positive promotion” for the US. PHOTO: REUTERS Published Oct 12, 2026, 08:20 AM Updated Oct 12, 2026, 08:55 AM Set as preferred source Listen WASHINGTON – A US judge on Oct 11 blocked the Trump administration from using taxpayer money to pay for political advertisements, after publicly funded television ads glorifying US President Donald Trump began airing in late September and sparked a bipartisan backlash. Manhattan-based US District Judge Jennifer Rochon temporarily barred the advertisements after plaintiffs including watchdog group Common Cause brought a lawsuit alleging the ads were political propaganda designed to help Republican candidates in the Nov 3 midterm elections, not public service announcements. The Trump administration was already planning to stop running the ads before Rochon’s order, according to a separate statement filed with the court on Oct 10. The decision caps days of controversy over the taxpayer-funded advertisements, which were aired in the final weeks before the midterm elections. “We won’t stop until this administration is held fully accountable, and no president from any party can waste and abuse taxpayer funds for propaganda ever again,” said Common Cause president and chief executive Virginia Kase Solomon.
